This website is the course support for Bioinformatics Tools, a practical course for MSc biology students at the University of Neuchâtel.
The course uses examples from genomics, microbial ecology, and plant biology, and introduces machine learning or deep learning as a tool for answering biological questions.

Getting started
This site collects the written supports for the nine sessions of the course. Each session has its own practical.qmd chapter with the exact steps to follow during the practical.

Format: nine sessions, 14:15-17:00 - about 45 min of theory, 1 h 50 of practice, 10 min break.
Level: deliberately simple and progressive; no prior programming experience is assumed.
Language: all written supports are in English.
Data: small teaching datasets are prepared in advance; no long installation or large download during class.


Course programme

Initial diagnostic and essential commands
Shell, biological formats, and quality control
Sequence similarity and phylogeny
Biological tables and visualisation with R
PCA and unsupervised learning
Supervised machine learning and evaluation
Introduction to deep learning
Guided project: question, script, and first result
Guided project: correction, interpretation, and presentation







ImportantAssessment



Sessions 1 and 2 are practice: they are not graded. The continuous assessment starts at Session 3: a short individual Moodle quiz (about 15 minutes) at the end of each session, based on the results actually obtained during the practical. The guided project (Sessions 8 and 9) is assessed separately.

NoteBiological question

TipStarting-point survey (about 4 min)



Before the lecture, fill in the short survey: starting-point survey, or scan the code below.

It asks about your background, the tools you have already met, and the data you care about. Your name is optional and the survey is not graded: the answers are used to weight the examples for the rest of the course, and the class summary is shown back to you a few minutes later so you can see how mixed the starting levels are.

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

identify your current folder and list its contents;
create and enter a folder;
copy a file and look inside it with head, tail, grep, and wc;
recognise FASTA records, count them reliably, and spot one that is not DNA or was truncated;
read an error message and correct the command;

title: 1  Session 1: Initial diagnostic and essential commands
text:
1.2 Theory (≈45 min)

1.2.1 1. Bioinformatics and the data it works on
Bioinformatics connects a biological question to data and to a reproducible analysis that produces a result you can explain.


Code
flowchart LR
  Q["Biological question<br/>(e.g. which genes respond to stress in this organism?)"] --> D["Data<br/>(files: FASTA, FASTQ, tables…)"]
  D --> A["Analysis<br/>(a few commands, run in order)"]
  A --> R["Result<br/>(a number, a table, a figure)"]
  R --> I["Interpretation<br/>(answer + one limitation)"]





flowchart LR
  Q["Biological question<br/>(e.g. which genes respond to stress in this organism?)"] --> D["Data<br/>(files: FASTA, FASTQ, tables…)"]
  D --> A["Analysis<br/>(a few commands, run in order)"]
  A --> R["Result<br/>(a number, a table, a figure)"]
  R --> I["Interpretation<br/>(answer + one limitation)"]






The analysis is just a list of commands run in a defined order. If you write the commands down, another person (including future you) can run them again and get the same result. That is what “reproducible” means, and it is the habit this course builds.

1.2.1.1 Where does biological data come from?
Different instruments answer different questions. You do not need to master any of these today: the goal is to recognise the main families and the kind of file each one lands in.










Data type
How it is produced
Typical files
Example question
In this course




Genome / amplicon sequencing
High-throughput sequencers (Illumina, Oxford Nanopore) read DNA fragments
FASTA, FASTQ
Which species are in this soil sample?
Sessions 2-3, 5-6


Bulk RNA-seq
Sequencing of RNA pooled from many cells → one expression value per gene
FASTQ → count table (CSV/TSV)
Which genes respond to drought?
Session 8 (project)


Single-cell RNA-seq
RNA sequenced per individual cell
sparse matrix (MTX, H5)
Which cell types are present, and how do they differ?
mentioned only


Proteomics
Mass spectrometry of peptides
mzML → abundance table
Which proteins change with treatment?
mentioned only


Metabolomics
Mass spectrometry or NMR of small molecules
feature-intensity tables
Which metabolites mark a phenotype?
mentioned only


Imaging / microscopy
Automated microscopes + image segmentation
TIFF / OME-TIFF → measurement tables
Does cell shape change between conditions?
mentioned only


Genotyping / GWAS
SNP arrays or sequencing → genotype matrix
VCF, genotype tables
Which variants associate with a trait?
Session 6 / project



The pattern to remember: whatever the instrument, the analysis almost always ends up in one of two shapes of text file: sequences (FASTA, FASTQ) or tables (rows = samples or features, columns = variables). This course spends its time teaching you to open, check, and summarise those two shapes with confidence.
Bulk vs single-cell, in one line each. Bulk measures the average over thousands of cells: cheap, and enough to ask “which genes differ between conditions”. Single-cell resolves cell-to-cell variation and rare populations: more expensive, and the data are much sparser. How the sequencing itself works (library preparation, paired-end reads, read length) comes in Session 2, alongside FASTQ and quality control.



1.2.2 2. How a computer works
A computer has a small number of parts. Each one has a single job.








Part
Job
Kitchen analogy




CPU (processor)
Does the calculations, one step after another (very fast).
The cook


RAM (memory)
Holds the data currently being worked on. Fast, but erased when the power goes off.
The worktop: only what you are using right now fits on it


Disk / SSD (storage)
Keeps files when the power is off. Slower than RAM, much bigger.
The fridge and cupboards


GPU (graphics card)
Does many simple calculations in parallel. Used for images and for deep learning.
A brigade of line cooks all chopping at once


Operating system (Linux, macOS, Windows)
Manages the parts, the files, and the programs.
The kitchen manager


Network card
Talks to other computers.
The delivery door



Two ideas matter for the rest of the course:

A program is just a file that the CPU knows how to run. ls, head, R and blast are all programs sitting on the disk.
Files live in folders, folders live in folders. The chain of folder names that leads to a file is its path, for example /home/you/bioinfo_course/data/reads.fasta. The leading / is the top of the tree. The folder you are “standing in” right now is the working directory; a command that is given no path looks there.


1.2.2.1 The shell
The shell lets you drive the computer by typing commands instead of clicking. You type the name of a program, press Enter, and read what it prints back. If you know R, this is the same idea with a different language. The shell we use is called bash. It is good at three things bioinformatics needs constantly: navigating files, repeating an analysis exactly, and moving or summarising large files automatically.



1.2.3 3. From your laptop to a compute cluster
A laptop is fine for writing code and looking at results. It is not fine for aligning a million sequencing reads: not enough CPU, not enough memory, and the data would not even fit. A compute cluster solves this. It is a set of powerful computers (“nodes”) in a server room that many people share, with the large data stored right next to them.
For this course we use LEGcompute, hosted by the Laboratory of Evolutionary Genetics and shared across the Institute of Biology (crolllab/IBIOL-compute-resources).



The LEGcompute cluster.









Resource
LEGcompute




CPU cores
~1000 (Intel + AMD)


GPUs
RTX 3090, 3× RTX A5500, 4× RTX 5000 Ada, 2× RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB)


Memory
4 TB RAM


Storage
80 TB SSD


System
Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, Slurm scheduler, RStudio Server




1.2.3.1 How the cluster is organised


Code
flowchart LR
  L["Your laptop"] -- "https :8787 (RStudio)" --> H
  L -- "ssh" --> H
  H["Login / head node<br/>(where you land)"] -- "sbatch / srun" --> S["Slurm scheduler"]
  S --> C1["compute node"]
  S --> C2["compute node"]
  S --> G["GPU node"]
  H --- ST[("Shared storage<br/>/home  /data  /scratch")]
  C1 --- ST
  C2 --- ST
  G --- ST





flowchart LR
  L["Your laptop"] -- "https :8787 (RStudio)" --> H
  L -- "ssh" --> H
  H["Login / head node<br/>(where you land)"] -- "sbatch / srun" --> S["Slurm scheduler"]
  S --> C1["compute node"]
  S --> C2["compute node"]
  S --> G["GPU node"]
  H --- ST[("Shared storage<br/>/home  /data  /scratch")]
  C1 --- ST
  C2 --- ST
  G --- ST







You log in to the head node. Everyone shares it, so it is for light interactive work only: editing, plotting, small commands (everything we do today).
Real jobs are submitted to Slurm with sbatch, which sends them to a free compute node so the machine is never overloaded and everyone gets a fair share. We meet Slurm properly in a later session.
Storage is shared by every node, so a file you create on the head node is visible in your jobs too:

/home/username: scripts and small files (quota: 100 GB per student);
/data/username: large datasets and analysis output (1+ TB);
/scratch: temporary space; files older than 30 days are deleted automatically.

~200 bioinformatics tools are pre-installed as modules (module load SAMtools). Nothing to install during class.







ImportantNo backups



No backup is made of anything on the server. Keeping a copy of work you care about is your responsibility.




1.2.3.2 Access for this course






ImportantConnecting to LEGcompute



1. Be on the university network. Either the unine WiFi on campus, or the GlobalProtect VPN from home. There is no way in from the open internet.
2. Claim your account. Open the shared Google Sheet the instructor. On the course tab, pick a free username and write your name in the yellow cell next to it. The first page of the sheet explains how to set or reset your password (via the user account server).
3. Connect (pick one):



Method
How
Good for




RStudio Server
Browser → http://legcompute.unine.ch:8787 → log in. Use the Terminal tab for the shell.
Everyone today. Nothing to install.


SSH
In a local terminal: ssh username@legcompute.unine.ch
Later, once you are comfortable.



We use RStudio Server for the whole course. It gives you an editor, an R Console, a Terminal and a file browser in one browser tab, with nothing to install.





1.2.4 4. The FASTA format
FASTA is the simplest way to store one or more biological sequences as text. A record has two parts:

a header line, whose first character is >, giving the sequence a name;
one or more sequence lines (the bases or amino acids).

>NC_045512.2 Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, surface glycoprotein region (partial)
ATGTTTGTTTTTCTTGTTTTATTGCCACTAGTCTCTAGTCAGTGTGTTAATCTTACAACC
AGAACTCAATTACCCCCTGCATACACTAATTCTTTCACACGTGGTGTTTATTACCCTGAC
>oligo_F short PCR primer
GATTACAGGCGTGAGCCACCACGT
Here the first record’s sequence is wrapped over two lines; the second fits on one. Both are still single records.
The next record starts at the next line beginning with >. Counting records is therefore the same as counting > lines. Nothing in the format tells you whether a sequence is DNA or protein, how long it is, or whether it is complete: you have to look.


1.2.5 Practical briefing
You will connect to the cluster, build a small project folder, and copy in one FASTA file, mystery.fasta. It is deliberately messy: different line widths, a record that is not DNA, and one that was cut off mid-download. Your job is to find that out with the commands, in pairs. Write every command you run into a script file, even (especially) the ones that fail: an error message is evidence, not a reason to start over.

text:
1.3 Practical (≈1 h 50)

1.3.1 Essential commands for today
Six commands to move around, plus four to look inside a file. That is the whole toolbox for today.








Command
What it does
Example




pwd
print working directory: “where am I?”
pwd


ls
list the current folder (ls -lh adds sizes)
ls -lh


mkdir
make a new folder
mkdir data


cd
change directory: move into a folder
cd data


cp
copy a file: cp <what> <where>
cp reads.fasta .


head
show the first lines of a text file
head -n 4 reads.fasta


tail
show the last lines
tail -n 3 reads.fasta


wc -l
count lines
wc -l reads.fasta


grep "^>"
show the lines that start with > (FASTA headers)
grep "^>" reads.fasta


grep -c "^>"
count the lines that start with > (records)
grep -c "^>" reads.fasta



^> means “a line beginning with >”. cat (whole file) and less (scroll, press q to quit) are useful too. Deleting files is deliberately not covered today.






TipThree habits that save time




Tab completion. Type the first few letters of a command or file name and press Tab. The shell finishes it for you and prevents typos.
Command history. Press ↑ to bring back the previous command and edit it.
Send a line from the script. With your .sh script open, put the cursor on a line and press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS) to run it in the Terminal without copy-pasting.





1.3.2 A. Connect and get oriented (15:00-15:15)

In a browser, go to http://legcompute.unine.ch:8787 and log in with your cluster username and password.



The RStudio Server login page.


Find these four parts of the RStudio window:

Source editor (top left): where scripts are written;
Console (bottom left): runs R code;
Terminal (a tab next to the Console): runs shell commands;
Files pane (bottom right): a click-through file browser.

If there is no Terminal tab, open one with Tools → Terminal → New Terminal. The welcome text it prints is just a message from the server.







WarningConsole vs Terminal



Everything in this practical is typed in the Terminal. The Console is for R and comes in later sessions. If a shell command gives a strange R error, you are in the wrong panel.



Open a new script: File → New File → Shell Script. Save it straight away as session_01_commands.sh. From now on, every command you try goes in this file, including ones that fail. Keep it: you reuse it in Session 2, and a partner reruns it in block F.







NoteIf you cannot connect



Do not lose ten minutes alone. Pair up with a neighbour and share one screen, or use a room computer, and tell the instructor. Fixing access for one person should not stop the class.




1.3.3 B. Where am I? Navigating folders (15:15-15:35)
Work one line at a time. Before you press Enter, write in your script, as a # comment, what you expect to see. Then run it and compare. A wrong prediction is the useful part: it shows exactly which idea to fix.
pwd                     # predict: which folder does this print?
ls                      # predict: what is already here?
mkdir bioinfo_course    # predict: what does ls show now?
cd bioinfo_course
pwd                     # predict: how has the path changed?
mkdir session_01
cd session_01
pwd






NoteCheckpoint



pwd ends in bioinfo_course/session_01.


Make a data folder and move into it. Predict each line first.
mkdir data
cd data
pwd






NoteCheckpoint



pwd ends in bioinfo_course/session_01/data. Check this before block C: the cp commands below copy into whatever folder you are currently standing in, so if pwd shows the wrong place, cd there first, or the files land somewhere you will not find them.




1.3.4 C. Get the data and take a first look (15:35-15:50)
Make sure pwd still ends in bioinfo_course/session_01/data (you are copying files into this folder, not into the course materials folder), then copy the sequence file and your worksheet, and check they arrived:
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_01/mystery.fasta .
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_01/WORKSHEET.md .
ls -lh
The final . means “here, in the current folder”. ls -lh also shows the file sizes.
WORKSHEET.md is a plain text file of questions, not a script: open it from the Files pane (click its name) or File → Open File, and type your answers directly under each “Answer:” line as you go through today’s blocks. Save it like any other file (Ctrl/Cmd+S). There is nothing to submit: it stays in your folder, and your instructor may look at it to see where the class is.
Now look inside it four ways. Predict the output of each line before you run it.
head -n 6 mystery.fasta       # the first few lines
tail -n 3 mystery.fasta       # the last few lines
grep -c "^>" mystery.fasta    # how many records (lines starting with >)
wc -l mystery.fasta           # how many lines in total






NoteCheckpoint



grep -c "^>" prints 40. wc -l prints 134. Keep both numbers: block D asks why they differ. Note the output of pwd and the ls -lh line for mystery.fasta now, for Section 2 of your worksheet.








TipMoving files in and out (no exercise, just so you know)



You will not need it today, but the RStudio Files pane moves files between your laptop and the server: Upload (laptop to server) and tick a file then More -> Export… (server to laptop). No scp required.



Uploading a file through the RStudio Files pane.






1.3.5 15:50-16:00: Checkpoint and short break
Before you step away: your script is saved, and pwd ends in bioinfo_course/session_01/data.


1.3.6 D. The investigation, in pairs (16:00-16:22)
mystery.fasta holds 40 records. Most are unremarkable filler; seven are not, and they are scattered in among the rest, not conveniently grouped at the top. Work with one other student. For each question below, write the answer and the command you used in Section 3 of your worksheet.

How many sequence records are in the file? Which command answers this without miscounting, and why is scrolling and counting > by eye unreliable here?
wc -l gave 134, not 80 (which would be two lines per record). Give the two separate reasons.
One record is not DNA. Which one? Give two clues, one from the sequence and one from the header.
One record was cut off during download. Which one, and how does tail show it?
Look at contig_07. Its sequence mixes UPPERCASE and lowercase and contains a run of N. What do the lowercase letters mean, and what does the N run mean? You do not need to change anything.
Which record has the shortest complete sequence? (The cut-off record from question 4 does not count: it has no sequence at all.) Show it and say how you decided. There is no single command that measures sequence length for you here: scroll through with cat or less, spot the records whose sequence fits on one line, and compare those by eye.







NoteShort on time?



At 16:22, move to block E with whatever you have, even if some questions are unanswered or your answers are unsure. Partial answers are fine: this is not graded, and there is no benefit in rushing block E to finish block D.








NoteCommands you may want





grep "^>" mystery.fasta          # list every header at once
grep -c "^>" mystery.fasta       # count records
head -n 20 mystery.fasta         # a first chunk of records, to get a feel for the file
tail -n 3 mystery.fasta          # last lines
grep -A 1 "SPIKE" mystery.fasta  # a matching header and the line right after it





1.3.7 E. Break it and diagnose, in pairs (16:22-16:40)
Every command below fails or surprises you, each for a different reason. For each one: predict what will happen, run it, copy the exact message, then write a version that works. Record all of it in your script.
cd Data
head mystery.fna
head -n mystery.fasta
cp mystery.fasta
cd mystery.fasta
head ../mystery.fasta
Hints:

Linux distinguishes uppercase from lowercase.
A file name must match exactly, extension included.
Some options need a value; some commands need more than one argument.
.. is “the folder above”; a bare name is “in the current folder”.

Return to bioinfo_course/session_01/data when you are done.






NoteShort on time?



At 16:40, move to block F even if you have not diagnosed all six. Whatever you have recorded, including the ones you did not solve, is still useful material for block G.




1.3.8 F. Reproduce it (16:40-16:50)
Trade session_01_commands.sh with your partner. From your home folder, start clean and run their commands in order:
cd ~
mkdir replay
cd replay
# now run your partner's commands, from the top, one by one
Does it run start to finish? If it stops, the missing step is something they did but did not write down, usually a cd or the cp path. Add the missing lines to your own script so it works from an empty folder. That is what “reproducible” means in practice.


1.3.9 G. Individual wrap-up (16:50-17:00)
On your own, complete Sections 1, 4, and 5 of your worksheet:

one command that failed today: the exact message, the cause, and the fix;
two or three sentences: from mystery.fasta alone, what can you say about these sequences, and what can you not say?

You should leave with:

WORKSHEET.md with your answers;
session_01_commands.sh with every command you attempted, errors included, that runs from a clean start.

Session 1 is a diagnostic, not a test. It is not graded: the continuous assessment (a short Moodle quiz at the end of each session) starts at Session 3. Your instructor may still look at your worksheet to see where the class is.
Keep the bioinfo_course folder. Session 2 reuses it.

For your own interest, not graded.

title: 1  Session 1: Initial diagnostic and essential commands
text:
1.6 Going further: more shell commands






TipOptional, if you have time left



Not part of the essential route, not graded, and nothing later in the course assumes you have done it. If you reach 16:50 and blocks A to G are done, work through as much of this as you like; stopping partway through is completely fine.


A few more small, useful commands. Try each one in bioinfo_course/session_01/data.

1.6.1 More ways to ls
ls -l     # long format: permissions, owner, size, date
ls -a     # include hidden files (names starting with a dot)
ls -h     # human-readable sizes, e.g. 6.4K instead of 6460
ls -lh    # options can be combined
ls -R     # list this folder and every folder inside it
Run each one and compare. Which combination would you reach for to check a file’s exact size before copying it somewhere with a tight quota?


1.6.2 Writing and reading small text files
echo prints text. On its own it writes to the screen; with > it writes to a file instead, replacing whatever was there. With >> it adds a line without erasing the rest.
echo "first line" > notes.txt
cat notes.txt              # cat shows the whole file at once
echo "second line" >> notes.txt
cat notes.txt
head -n 1 notes.txt        # compare with cat: only the first line
> and >> are two characters apart and easy to mix up: > replacing a file you meant to add to is a classic way to lose work, so pause before you press Enter on one.


1.6.3 Moving and renaming with mv
cp leaves the original in place; mv does not; it moves or renames.
mkdir backup
cp mystery.fasta backup/
ls backup/
mv backup/mystery.fasta backup/mystery_copy.fasta   # mv also renames
ls backup/


1.6.4 Two more worth knowing exist

less mystery.fasta scrolls a file a screen at a time with the arrow keys; press q to quit. Handy for a file too long for head to feel like enough.
nano notes.txt opens a small in-terminal text editor: type, Ctrl+X to exit, y to save. You already have an editor in RStudio’s Source pane, so you may never need it here, but you will meet nano again on other servers.

1.7 Answers






NoteOpen this after you have tried the exercises yourself





Session 1 is not graded, so there is no reason to hide the answers once you have genuinely tried each block. Use this to check your own reasoning, not instead of it: the value is in working out why, not in reading the line below.
Block C checkpoint. grep -c "^>" mystery.fasta prints 40; wc -l mystery.fasta prints 134.
Block D, the investigation.

40 records, from grep -c "^>" mystery.fasta. Counting > by eye is unreliable here because 40 headers are spread over 134 unevenly wrapped lines: easy to double-count or skip one while scrolling.
wc -l gives 134, not 80 (2 x 40), for two reasons: (a) most sequences wrap over two or more lines, adding lines beyond one per record; (b) truncated_record contributes only its header line, with no sequence line at all.
Not DNA: sp|P0DTC2|SPIKE_SARS2. Sequence clue: it contains letters that are not A/C/G/T/N (E, F, I, K, L, M, P, Q, R, S, V, W, Y). Header clue: sp|...| is a UniProt (Swiss-Prot) protein identifier, and the description says “glycoprotein”.
Truncated: truncated_record. tail -n 3 mystery.fasta shows the file ending on a header line, with no sequence line after it.
In contig_07, lowercase letters mark soft-masked regions (repetitive sequence flagged by a masking tool, not removed). The run of N is an assembly gap: the length is estimated but the bases are unknown.
Shortest complete sequence: oligo_F (24 bases, one line). truncated_record has no sequence at all, so it counts as “cut off” (question 4), not “shortest”.

Block E, six failures.








Command
Fails because
A version that works




cd Data
case sensitivity: the folder is data
cd data


head mystery.fna
wrong name: the file is mystery.fasta
head mystery.fasta


head -n mystery.fasta
-n needs a number; it consumed mystery.fasta as the count
head -n 5 mystery.fasta


cp mystery.fasta
cp needs a destination as well as a source
cp mystery.fasta backup.fasta


cd mystery.fasta
mystery.fasta is a file, not a directory
cd . (stay), or cd .. to go up


head ../mystery.fasta (from data/)
.. is session_01/, where the file is not
head mystery.fasta or head ./mystery.fasta



Optional challenge.

A. Vitis_vinifera.12Xv2.dna.toplevel.fa is 472 MB with 20 sequences (grep -c "^>"). head and grep -c both return in well under a second even on a file this size. Opening it in a text editor would try to load the whole 472 MB into memory at once, instead of reading a few bytes at a time.

text:
2.2 Theory (≈45 min)

2.2.1 1. The FASTQ format
FASTA (Session 1) only stores a sequence and its name. FASTQ stores that plus, for every single base, how much the sequencer trusts its own reading. Each record is exactly four lines:
@SRR098281.1 length=36
GATTTGGGGTTCAAAGCAGTATCGATCAAATAGTAA
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII







Line
Content




1
@ + read name and, sometimes, extra info


2
the sequence itself (A/C/G/T, same alphabet as FASTA)


3
a bare + (sometimes repeats the name; ignore it)


4
one quality character per base in line 2, same length as line 2



So a FASTQ record is a FASTA record with a fourth line bolted on. Counting records is the same idea as Session 1, but the count of > lines becomes a count of every 4th line instead, since there is no unique marker character to grep for FASTQ headers as cleanly as ^> did.


2.2.2 2. What a quality score actually is
Line 4 looks like punctuation soup. It is not. Each character encodes a Phred quality score: the sequencer’s own estimate of how likely it is that this one base was read wrong. Higher score = more confident. The character is just that number, hidden as a single symbol so line 2 and line 4 line up one-for-one.
You will not need the formula, only the reading direction: some characters mean “trust this”, others mean “doubt this”. Modern Illumina sequencers do not even give a smooth range any more: they round every base into one of a handful of confidence bins. Six of those characters, low to high:



Character
Phred score
Roughly means




!
0
no confidence at all


#
2
very likely wrong


,
11
doubtful


:
25
acceptable


F
37
good


I
40
excellent









TipDecode two bases by hand (2 min)



Take ,IF# (four bases). Using the table: which base would you trust least, and which one most? You just did, by hand, exactly what a quality-control tool does automatically for every base of every read, thousands of times per second.


Nobody reads quality lines by eye on real data: a run produces millions of reads. A tool called FastQC does the same decoding, then plots the score by position along the read, across all reads in the file at once, and gives you a report instead of a wall of symbols. That plot is today’s main practical output, on data you fetch and run yourself.


2.2.3 3. Worked example: 50,000 generations of E. coli
Since 1988, Richard Lenski’s lab has kept twelve populations of E. coli growing continuously in a glucose-limited flask, transferred to a fresh flask every single day. This is the Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE): the longest-running controlled evolution experiment there is, now well past 50,000 generations. One population, Ara-3, did something nobody expected: around generation 31,500, it evolved the ability to feed on citrate, a molecule the ancestral strain could not use as food under the experiment’s conditions. Evolution, caught in the act, in a flask.
Today’s data are real sequencing reads from this experiment, at three points in its history: 5,000, 15,000, and 50,000 generations. Before anyone can ask an evolutionary question with them (“did anything change in the DNA between these timepoints?”), the same unglamorous first step applies as to any sequencing data: check whether the reads themselves are trustworthy. That is today’s job. The evolutionary question itself is not ours to answer today, but you are handling the actual reads behind a real, famous result.


2.2.4 Practical briefing
You will rebuild your project folder from Session 1, fetch three small E. coli FASTQ files (one per generation) plus a very good and a very bad reference sample, and run FastQC on all five. You then build a checklist of what a “bad” report looks like from the two references, and use it to judge the real E. coli data and to make a keep/flag call on a sample you have not seen before. Everything you run and every decision you make goes in your script and worksheet, exactly like Session 1.

2.3 Practical (≈1 h 50)

2.3.1 New commands for today
Three new commands on top of everything from Session 1 (pwd, ls, mkdir, cd, cp, head, tail, wc -l, grep, cat, less).








Command
What it does
Example




mv
move or rename a file (unlike cp, the original does not stay behind)
mv a.txt results/


module load
make a pre-installed tool available in this session
module load FastQC


fastqc
run quality control on one or more FASTQ files, producing an HTML report
fastqc sample.fastq.gz









ImportantCheck the module name before class



module load FastQC follows the pattern from Session 1 (module load SAMtools), but the exact name and capitalisation on LEGcompute must be confirmed with module avail fastqc before the session; instructor to update this block if it differs.




2.3.2 A. Rebuild the project and fetch the data (15:00-15:15)
Reopen bioinfo_course from Session 1. Predict each line before running it.
cd ~/bioinfo_course
mkdir session_02
cd session_02
mkdir data results
cd data
pwd






NoteCheckpoint



pwd ends in bioinfo_course/session_02/data, and bioinfo_course/session_02 now contains two empty folders, data and results. Keeping raw files and generated output apart like this is the whole of “project organisation” for today: two folders, used consistently.


Copy in the three timepoints, two reference files, and your worksheet:
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_02/ecoli_5k.fastq.gz .
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_02/ecoli_15k.fastq.gz .
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_02/ecoli_50k.fastq.gz .
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_02/reference_good.fastq.gz .
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_02/reference_bad.fastq.gz .
cp /home/cmaslard/bioinfo_tools_course/session_02/WORKSHEET.md .
ls -lh
The two reference_ files are not from the E. coli experiment: they are the official “very good” and “very bad” example reads from the FastQC authors, cut down to 10,000 reads each. You will use them in block D as a yardstick, so you can see what a clean run and a failing run actually look like before judging the real E. coli data.






TipWhy .gz?





Sequencing files are big, so they are almost always shipped compressed. zcat reads a .gz file without decompressing it first, e.g. zcat ecoli_5k.fastq.gz | head -n 4. fastqc also accepts .gz files directly: no need to decompress anything today.





2.3.3 B. Look inside a FASTQ file (15:15-15:35)
Predict the output of each line before running it.
zcat ecoli_5k.fastq.gz | head -n 4     # the first record, all four lines
zcat ecoli_5k.fastq.gz | wc -l         # total lines






NoteCheckpoint



The first line starts with @. The third line is a bare +. Line 2 and line 4 are the same length. wc -l divided by 4 gives the number of reads in the file: write that number, and the file’s ls -lh size, in Section 2 of your worksheet, for all three files.


Now decode a real quality string by hand, using the table from Theory 2:
zcat ecoli_5k.fastq.gz | head -n 4 | tail -n 1   # just the quality line of read 1
Pick any three consecutive characters from that line. Look each one up in the table and write down the three Phred scores. Would you trust that stretch of the read? You now know exactly what FastQC’s main plot is going to show you, one read at a time, for every read in the file at once.


2.3.4 C. Run FastQC (15:35-15:50)
module load FastQC
fastqc ecoli_5k.fastq.gz ecoli_15k.fastq.gz ecoli_50k.fastq.gz reference_good.fastq.gz reference_bad.fastq.gz -o ../results
ls -lh ../results
-o ../results sends the reports to the results folder instead of cluttering data, the same separation you set up in block A. Each input file produces two outputs: an _fastqc.html report and an _fastqc.zip archive (the report’s data, unpacked; ignore it today).






NoteCheckpoint



../results contains ten files: five _fastqc.html and five _fastqc.zip, one pair per input file. fastqc finished without an error message for all five.


Download the five HTML reports through the RStudio Files pane (tick each file → More → Export…, as in Session 1) and open them in a browser on your own laptop.


2.3.5 15:50-16:00: Checkpoint and short break
Before you step away: five FastQC reports open (or downloaded), your script saved, and your three E. coli read counts and file sizes recorded in the worksheet.


2.3.6 D. Quality doctor, in pairs (16:00-16:40)
A FastQC report has many sections; three matter today.








Section
What it shows
Red flag looks like




Per base sequence quality
a green/orange/red band, quality score by position along the read
the line dips into orange or red, especially toward the end


Per sequence GC content
one smooth bump expected, centred on the organism’s typical GC%
a second bump, or a bump far from the expected centre


Overrepresented sequences
short sequences appearing far more often than chance
a long list here, especially of adapter-like sequences



First, build your eye for a real failure. Open the reports you just made for reference_good and reference_bad, side by side. Look at “Per base sequence quality”: one line stays high and flat, the other sinks toward the end of the read.






NoteWhy these two look a little different from the E. coli reads



The reference reads are older Illumina data: 40 bases long (the E. coli reads are about 150) and stored with an older quality encoding. FastQC detects that automatically, so the plots are directly comparable. Decode quality characters by hand only on the E. coli files, as in block B: the table in Theory 2 is for the modern encoding.


The Babraham authors publish the full-size versions of these same two reports, if you want to see every section at full depth: good and bad.
For each of the three sections above, write one sentence describing the difference between reference_good and reference_bad. That sentence is your checklist for the rest of the practical.
Now open your own reports for the two extreme timepoints, 5,000 and 50,000 generations (leave 15,000 unopened; that one is block E), and with your partner answer in Section 3 of your worksheet:

Using your checklist, does either timepoint look like reference_bad in any section? Which one, and which section? Does either look as clean as reference_good? Real data is rarely either extreme.
Compare “Per base sequence quality” between the two. Does read quality change with generation number, or does it look the same regardless of how evolutionarily old or young the sample is? What does that tell you about what sequencing quality actually depends on (the sequencing run) versus what it does not depend on (the biology of the sample)?
Pick the single plot you found most convincing for deciding whether to trust a sample. Why that one over the others?







NoteShort on time?



At 16:40, move to block E with whatever you have. A partial checklist and one solid observation per timepoint are enough to start block E.




2.3.7 E. Individual: a new sample (16:40-16:55)
On your own, open the report for 15,000 generations, the one timepoint you fetched and ran FastQC on in blocks A-C but have not yet individually assessed.
Using your checklist from block D, write in Section 4 of your worksheet:

your decision: trust this sample for downstream analysis, or flag it;
two observations from the report that support your decision, each naming the section you looked at.

This is the exact shape of decision a bioinformatician makes before every real analysis, and the exact shape of answer the graded Moodle quizzes from Session 3 onward will ask for: a decision, backed by named evidence, not a gut feeling.


2.3.8 Wrap-up (16:55-17:00)
You should leave with:

WORKSHEET.md, Sections 2-4 completed;
session_02_commands.sh with every command you ran;
bioinfo_course/session_02/results/, containing three FastQC reports.

Session 2 is still not graded: the continuous assessment starts at Session 3. Keep the bioinfo_course folder; Session 3 uses it again.

text:
2.6 Answers






NoteOpen this after you have tried the exercises yourself





Session 2 is not graded, so there is no reason to hide the answers once you have genuinely tried each block. Use this to check your own reasoning, not instead of it: the value is in working out why, not in reading the line below. These are the real FastQC numbers from the five files, not a schematic version of them.
Block D, question 1 (does either timepoint look like reference_bad?). Not in the same way. reference_bad fails “Per base sequence quality” early (mean quality is already drifting down by position 4), fails “Per tile sequence quality”, and warns on “Overrepresented sequences” (four overlapping 41-base sequences, each about 0.5-0.65% of all reads, flagged “No Hit”: the same piece of DNA, read many times). Both E. coli timepoints also fail “Per base sequence quality”, but only because of the last 20-30 bases of a 150-base read (mean quality falls from about 32 at position 1 to about 22-23 by position 150); the first 120 bases stay solidly in the green zone, and neither timepoint flags a single overrepresented sequence. Neither looks as clean as reference_good, which passes “Per base sequence quality” outright across its full 40 bases.
Block D, question 2 (does quality change with generation number?). No, essentially not. 5,000 generations: mean Phred ≈32.4 at position 1, ≈22.8 at position 150. 50,000 generations: mean Phred ≈31.6 at position 1, ≈21.9 at position 150. Same shape, same collapse point, within about one Phred point of each other. That is the point: sequencing quality is a property of the sequencing run (the chemistry, the read’s position on the flow cell), not of the DNA’s evolutionary age. A population at 50,000 generations is not “worse DNA”; it was simply sequenced the same way as the others.
Block D, question 3 (most convincing plot). For this dataset, “Per base sequence quality” is the only one of the three sections that actually separates the files. “Per sequence GC content” warns on reference_good and on all three E. coli files alike, and even passes on reference_bad, so it does not reliably tell a trustworthy sample from a failing one here. “Overrepresented sequences” stays clean on every E. coli file. Reasonable answers vary, but they should name a specific numeric or visual feature of the quality plot, not just “it looked bad”.
Block E (15,000 generations). The report sits exactly where the pattern from block D predicts: mean Phred ≈32.5 at position 1, falling to ≈22.8 by position 150 (“Per base sequence quality” fails, the same tail-collapse shape as the other two timepoints); “Per sequence GC content” warns, but the peak sits around 52-54%, in range for E. coli’s genome; “Overrepresented sequences” passes, with nothing flagged. A defensible decision is trust, with the last 20-30 bases trimmed: the problem is confined to the read ends, not scattered through the whole read or paired with a contamination signal, so this is not the same kind of failure as reference_bad. “Flag outright” is defensible too, as long as it is backed by two named observations rather than a single section.
Optional challenge A. All three files contain exactly 10,000 reads each (zcat ... | wc -l gives 40,000 for every file, divided by 4). That equality is not a property of the original sequencing runs: it was built in on purpose when these class files were subsampled from the much larger original runs, specifically so a depth difference could not be mistaken for a quality difference today. For a genuinely fair comparison between two arbitrary samples, you would need to confirm the depth matches yourself first, exactly as you just did here, rather than assume it.
Optional challenge B. For example:
cd ~/bioinfo_course/session_02/results
mkdir gen5000 gen15000 gen50000
mv ecoli_5k_fastqc.* gen5000/
mv ecoli_15k_fastqc.* gen15000/
mv ecoli_50k_fastqc.* gen50000/
ls -R ..

text:
Bonus: watching evolution happen (variant calling)






TipOptional, for students who are ahead



This is not part of the course. No marks depend on it, and no later session assumes you have done it. It exists because it directly answers a question today’s practical raises but does not close: the DNA behind these reads has been evolving for 50,000 generations, so what, exactly, changed? A bacterial genome is small (4.6 Mb, against 3+ billion for ours), so the full path from reads to an answer takes well under a minute.


FastQC told you whether to trust a read. Variant calling goes one step further: it lines every read up against a reference genome and reports every position where your sample disagrees with it. Each disagreement is a candidate mutation. Four new tools, each doing one job:







Tool
Job




bwa index
prepares a reference genome for fast searching


bwa mem
aligns reads against that reference


samtools sort / index
puts aligned reads in genome order and makes them searchable


bcftools mpileup / call
at every position, compares the reads to the reference and reports differences




2.7.1 Try it (about 15 minutes)
Work in a new folder, and reuse the module load habit from earlier today.
mkdir -p ~/bioinfo_course/session_02/bonus_evolution
cd ~/bioinfo_course/session_02/bonus_evolution
module load BWA/0.7.18-GCCcore-13.3.0 SAMtools/1.21-GCC-13.3.0 BCFtools/1.21-GCC-13.3.0
1. Get the ancestor. Every mutation is defined relative to a starting point: the LTEE’s ancestral strain, REL606, whose genome is public on NCBI (accession NC_012967.1).
curl -s "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=nuccore&id=NC_012967.1&rettype=fasta&retmode=text" -o REL606.fasta
bwa index REL606.fasta
2. Get a deeper read sample. The 10,000-read files from earlier today are enough for quality control, but too shallow to call mutations confidently. Reuse the same zcat | head | gzip trick from block B, just with a bigger number, on the 50,000-generation run:
curl -s "ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/fastq/SRR258/006/SRR2584866/SRR2584866_1.fastq.gz" | zcat | head -n 800000 | gzip > reads_deep.fastq.gz






NoteCheckpoint before continuing



zcat reads_deep.fastq.gz | wc -l prints 800000. Downloads over a real network occasionally cut short with no error message; if your number is much smaller, just run the curl line again.


3. Align, sort, and index.
bwa mem -t 4 REL606.fasta reads_deep.fastq.gz | samtools sort -o aligned.bam -
samtools index aligned.bam
samtools flagstat aligned.bam
flagstat reports what fraction of reads found a matching spot in the reference. Expect well above 90%: this is the ancestor’s own species, after all, just 50,000 generations later.
4. Call variants.
bcftools mpileup -f REL606.fasta aligned.bam | bcftools call -mv -Oz -o variants.vcf.gz
bcftools index variants.vcf.gz
zcat variants.vcf.gz | grep -vc "^#"
bcftools view variants.vcf.gz | grep -v "^##" | head -10
Each remaining line is one candidate difference from the ancestor: a position (POS), what the ancestor had (REF), what your sample has instead (ALT), and a confidence score (QUAL). Sort by quality to see where you should look first:
bcftools view variants.vcf.gz | grep -v "^#" | sort -t$'\t' -k6,6 -rn | head -5






ImportantRead this before you get excited



This list is a rough first pass, not a validated result. At this depth and with no filtering, some entries are real mutations and some are noise (a handful of misread bases lining up by chance). The actual published analysis of this experiment (Tenaillon et al., Science, 2016) uses much deeper coverage, both directions of each paired-end read, and careful filtering. Treat today’s list as “here is what the first step of a real analysis looks like”, not as a discovery.




2.7.2 Go further

Repeat steps 2-4 for SRR2589044 (5,000 generations) and SRR2584863 (15,000 generations). Does the number of candidate variants grow with generation number, the way you would expect if mutations accumulate over time?
Filter by quality before counting: bcftools view -i 'QUAL>50' variants.vcf.gz | grep -vc "^#". How much does the count drop?
The famous result from this population, Ara-3, is that it evolved the ability to use citrate aerobically, around generation 31,500 (Blount, Borland & Lenski, PNAS 2008). The paper is short and readable end to end: the team tested 8.4 trillion ancestral cells for the ability to grow on citrate and found not one that could, yet a clone from generation 31,500 could. Nothing in today’s bonus identifies that specific mutation: it involves a structural rearrangement, not a simple substitution, and needs the full genome assembly and paired-end reads to see properly. This bonus shows you the first step of the method that eventually finds it.

Bonus: version control with Git






TipOptional, for students who are ahead



This is not part of the course. No marks depend on it, and no later session assumes you have done it. It is here because version control becomes genuinely useful once your analyses grow past a couple of scripts. Come back to it whenever you like.


You already keep a command log and clear file names. Git is the professional version of that same habit: it records your project as a series of snapshots (“commits”), each with a short message.
Three things this gives you:

A history you can trust. Every commit is a labelled state of the whole project. You can see exactly what changed between two points and go back to any earlier one. No more analysis_final_v3_really_final.R.
A clean off-site backup. One git push copies your project, with its full history, to GitHub. Useful anywhere, and especially on the cluster, which is not backed up (see Session 1).
Sharing by link. A repository is a URL. Send it and another person has your exact code and history; they can read it, rerun it, or suggest changes without a single emailed zip file.


2.7.3 The idea in four steps


Code
flowchart LR
  W["Working folder<br/>(your files)"] -- "git add" --> S["Staged<br/>(marked for the next snapshot)"]
  S -- "git commit -m '...'" --> C["Commit<br/>(snapshot + message, saved locally)"]

Download the lecture slides (PDF)
Sessions 1 and 2 taught you to look inside a sequence file and to judge whether its reads can be trusted. text:
3.2 Theory (≈45 min)

3.2.1 1. Similarity search: what BLAST actually measures
grep (Sessions 1-2) finds exact text. Biological sequences almost never match exactly: mutation, sequencing error, and evolutionary divergence all change a handful of bases here and there. BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) finds sequences that are similar enough, scores how similar, and does it against thousands of sequences at once, in seconds.
Given one query sequence and a set of reference sequences, blastn reports one row per match it considers meaningful:







Column
Meaning




pident
percent identity: of the aligned bases, what fraction are identical


length
how many bases the alignment covers


evalue
how many matches this good would be expected by chance alone; smaller is better, 0.0 means effectively impossible by chance


bitscore
an overall match quality score, normalized so it is comparable between searches; higher is better



A high pident over a short length can still be a coincidence; a lower pident over a long length with a tiny evalue usually is not. Reading a BLAST hit means looking at these together, not just the percent identity on its own. Block B gives you a real case where trusting pident alone would mislead you.






TipWhere you have already seen this idea



Session 1’s mystery.fasta contained one record, sp|P0DTC2|SPIKE_SARS2, that was neither obviously DNA nor identifiable by eye. A similarity search is exactly the next step you would take on a record like that: not “does it look like DNA”, but “what does it match”. You meet that exact sequence again at the end of this theory block.


Search settings matter, too. BLAST can run in a fast, strict mode tuned for near-identical sequences, or a slower, more sensitive mode that also reports weaker, more distant matches. Neither is “wrong”; they answer slightly different questions, and today’s practical uses both, deliberately, one after the other.


3.2.2 2. From one match to a tree
BLAST answers “what is my sequence most similar to”, one hit at a time. A phylogenetic tree goes further: it places every sequence you give it, including ones too different from each other for a strict BLAST search to confidently match, on a single diagram of relative relatedness. Three steps get you there:

Multiple sequence alignment. Every sequence is stacked and padded with gaps (-) so that the same column means the same position in every sequence. Session 2’s FASTQ lines were already the same length by construction; here, alignment is the step that creates that correspondence across sequences that differ in length.
Distance. Once sequences line up column by column, counting the fraction of columns that differ between every pair of sequences gives a distance: more differences, more distant. Doing this for every pair at once gives a distance matrix, one number per pair; today you will read it as a table, the same idea scales to a colour-coded heatmap for larger datasets than today’s.
Tree building. An algorithm arranges sequences on a tree so that closely related sequences sit together, joined by a recent common node. Today’s tool, FastTree, does this quickly even for larger alignments than ours, using a statistical (approximately maximum-likelihood) model rather than the distance matrix alone, and it reports a support value at each split: roughly, how confident the method is that this grouping is real rather than an artefact of this particular alignment.







TipReading a tree










Term
Meaning




Tip
one sequence, labelled, at the end of a branch


Node
a point where branches split: the inferred common ancestor of everything beyond it


Branch length
genetic distance (not necessarily time) between a node and the sequence or node it leads to


Clade
a node plus everything descended from it: a complete sub-group


Outgroup
a sequence known to be the most distantly related, used to anchor which end of the tree is the root


Support value
confidence (here, 0 to 1) that a given split is real, from resampling the alignment many times and checking how often the same split reappears



Two tips drawn close together are closely related because of where their shared node is, not because they happen to be printed near each other. Always trace back to the node.


FastTree’s speed comes from heuristics, not from skipping statistics: it is a fast, reasonable first answer, not the last word on a dataset this size. One known weakness, relevant for today’s most distant sequences: raw percent-difference, the simplest possible distance, underestimates true evolutionary distance once enough time has passed for the same site to mutate more than once (“saturation”). Distance correction models (for example Jukes-Cantor) attempt to account for this. A full, maximum-likelihood tree with properly resampled bootstrap support (rather than FastTree’s faster approximation) is the published standard, and out of scope for today, but the optional challenge lets you try a correction model on today’s data.


3.2.3 3. Worked example: a family of coronaviruses
Coronaviruses that infect humans are not one thing: SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-1 (the 2003 SARS outbreak), MERS-CoV, and several seasonal “common cold” coronaviruses are all related, but to very different degrees. Some share a recent common ancestor; others split off much earlier. Comparing one gene, the spike gene (S), the gene for the protein coronaviruses use to enter a host cell, across several of these viruses is a standard way virologists work out exactly that: which ones are close relatives, and which are more like distant cousins. That is precisely today’s practical, on real sequences from these real viruses, checked at both the nucleotide and the protein level.






TipTwo-minute detour: the same logic on a protein, via UniProt



Session 1’s unidentified record, sp|P0DTC2|SPIKE_SARS2, is the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. P0DTC2 is its accession in UniProt, a curated protein database: look it up and, instead of raw sequence, you get functional annotation: named domains (receptor-binding domain, furin cleavage site, signal peptide, transmembrane region), and links to solved 3D structures. A protein search (blastp) works exactly like blastn, just on amino acids instead of bases; block D2 has you run it on this exact protein.




3.2.4 Practical briefing
You will fetch one unidentified sequence (unknown_sample.fasta) and four named reference sequences, all spike genes from different coronaviruses. You will BLAST the unknown against the references yourself, at two sensitivity settings, inspect a prepared alignment and distance matrix by hand, render and annotate a prepared tree in R, and finally repeat the comparison at the protein level. Everything you run goes in your command log, exactly like Sessions 1-2.

3.3.1 New commands for today
Nine new commands on top of everything from Sessions 1-2: today’s practical went past this course’s usual limit of six, on purpose, because block D now has you fetch real data from NCBI yourselves rather than start from a prepared file. 3.3.3 B. Two searches, quick then deep (15:15-15:35)
module load BLAST+
makeblastdb -in reference_spike_genes.fasta -dbtype nucl -out ../results/spike_db
blastn -query unknown_sample.fasta -db ../results/spike_db -outfmt 6 -out ../results/blast_result.tsv
cat ../results/blast_result.tsv
-outfmt 6 requests a plain tab-separated table, in this column order:
qseqid  sseqid  pident  length  mismatch  gapopen  qstart  qend  sstart  send  evalue  bitscore






NoteCheckpoint



blast_result.tsv has exactly one line: unknown_sample against SARS-CoV-2_Wuhan-Hu-1, at roughly 93% identity over essentially the whole gene (length ≈ 3,800), with evalue 0.0. Only one reference produced a hit at all under these default (strict) search settings; the other three did not even appear in the table.


A strict search can tell you “nothing” about a real relationship, not because there is none, but because the match fell below what the search was tuned to report. Run a second, more sensitive search against the same database:
blastn -query unknown_sample.fasta -db ../results/spike_db -task blastn -evalue 1e-3 -max_hsps 1 -outfmt 6 -out ../results/blast_result_deep.tsv
cat ../results/blast_result_deep.tsv
-task blastn switches from the strict default algorithm to the standard, more sensitive one; -evalue 1e-3 relaxes how significant a match must be to get reported; -max_hsps 1 keeps only each reference’s single best-scoring match.






NoteCheckpoint



This time, blast_result_deep.tsv has four lines, one per reference. Look closely at length, evalue, and bitscore, not just pident, for the two weakest hits (MERS-CoV and HCoV-OC43_seasonal). One of the two has a higher pident than the other, but a shorter length, a weaker evalue, and a lower bitscore. Which one actually looks like the better-supported match, and why? Write your answer in Section 2 of your worksheet: this is the real case the theory block warned you about.

head -5 aligned_spike.fasta

3.3.6 D. Fetch real NCBI data and build a tree, for real (16:00-16:40, pairs)
So far every file has been prepared for you. For this one block, you fetch the sequences yourselves, straight from NCBI, and build a tree from data nobody has cleaned up for you first. You will also add unknown_sample into this much bigger tree: does it land inside the real SARS-CoV-2 diversity, or outside it, as its own separate branch? This is an independent check on blocks B-D2’s conclusion, by a completely different method.
This block has more to do than today’s others, on purpose, now that you are working with a real public database instead of a prepared file. It is fine if you do not finish everything before 16:40: get the tree itself built and plotted first, that is the required part; the questions below it in WORKSHEET.md can be finished before Thursday, the same as Section 5.
First, see how big this search really is, before limiting it to something you can download in a few minutes:

NoteCheckpoint

Now fetch a manageable subset: 100 of those, plus 13 specific named variants by accession, plus unknown_sample itself, already sitting in your data folder since block A:

Now plot it. plot_tree.R reads ../results/sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk, roots it on unknown_sample (a real outgroup this time, not a SARS-CoV-2 genome itself), and labels the 13 named variants and unknown_sample in colour; the other 100 tips stay thin and grey, real background diversity rather than something to identify. Three things to confirm: first, unknown_sample sits on a branch far longer than any other, dozens of times longer than a typical branch between two SARS-CoV-2 genomes — it is related to the rest of the tree, but clearly not one of them, the same conclusion blocks B-D2 reached by a completely different method. Second, the Omicron sublineages (BA.1 through 24C) should all fall within one connected part of the tree, separate from the earlier named variants (Alpha, Delta, Gamma, Mu) — consistent with Omicron descending from a single common ancestor. Third, Delta should be the named variant branching closest to Wuhan-Hu-1, before Mu, Alpha, Gamma, and Omicron.


Open the root_on line near the top of the script, change it from "unknown_sample" to "MN908947.1" (Wuhan-Hu-1), and run the script again.






NoteCheckpoint



The named variants still group with each other exactly as before: rerooting never changes who is related to whom, only which tip sits at the very top of the plot. But this particular reroot should look messier than the original: Wuhan-Hu-1 is itself one of the 113 SARS-CoV-2 genomes, not a real outgroup, so forcing the tree to start there is a weaker choice than rooting on unknown_sample, which actually sits outside the group being compared. Change root_on back to "unknown_sample" before exporting.


Export the figure: in the Plots pane, Export → Save as Image… (or Save as PDF…), into results/. Any format the dialog offers is fine to submit (PNG, JPEG, SVG, PDF, …): Moodle accepts all of them, there is no single required file type here. Set the height generously, at least 14 inches (or ~1400 px) if you are offered a choice: 114 labelled and unlabelled tips need the extra room to stay legible, more than the on-screen preview shows. This tree image is today’s required figure for block D.






NoteShort on time?



If the fetch, MAFFT, or FastTree did not finish, change the file name near the top of plot_tree.R from "../results/sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk" to "sars_variants_tree.nwk", the prepared fallback copied in block A, and continue from there.


In Section 4 of WORKSHEET.md, write a few sentences describing your tree image, the same way you would in a lab notebook: where unknown_sample sits and how its branch compares to the rest; whether the named variants fall in the order you would expect; and, using the collection date you looked up earlier, to what era do most of your 100 background sequences most likely belong — recent, or as old as the earliest named variants? (Hint: check a handful of background headers in sars_variants.fasta with grep ">" sars_variants.fasta | head, and compare the years you see there to MN908947.1’s collection date.) The image file itself is submitted alongside WORKSHEET.md, not pasted into it.
If you have more time: unknown_sample is the longest branch by far, but it is not the only one worth a second look — among the 100 background sequences, one or two are still noticeably longer than most. Real NCBI submissions are not curated the way today’s other files are: what might explain a real sequence standing out like that (a sequencing or assembly error, a genuinely unusual isolate, a mislabelled sample)? There is no single correct answer; this is the kind of judgement call real analyses require.


3.3.7 D2. The same question, at the protein level (16:40-16:50, pairs)
reference_spike_proteins.fasta holds the same four coronaviruses’ spike proteins, including the exact Session 1 record, SARS-CoV-2_Wuhan-Hu-1 (UniProt P0DTC2). Build a protein database and search the file against itself:
makeblastdb -in reference_spike_proteins.fasta -dbtype prot -out ../results/protein_db
blastp -query reference_spike_proteins.fasta -db ../results/protein_db -max_hsps 1 -outfmt "6 qseqid sseqid pident length evalue bitscore" -out ../results/blastp_result.tsv
cat ../results/blastp_result.tsv
Each sequence is searched against all four, including itself, so ignore the self-hits (pident 100: a sequence always matches itself perfectly).






NoteCheckpoint



blastp_result.tsv has 16 lines: four references, each searched against all four (including itself), one best match per pair. Find the line pairing SARS-CoV-2_Wuhan-Hu-1 with SARS-CoV-1_Tor2: percent identity at the protein level. Compare it with the same pair’s percent identity at the nucleotide level, from block B’s deep search (blast_result_deep.tsv). Protein identity comes out a little higher. Several different DNA codons can encode the same amino acid: a nucleotide substitution that lands on one of those “silent” positions changes the gene without changing the protein. Write this comparison, with both numbers, in Section 4 of your worksheet.




3.3.8 E. Draft your interpretation; submit on Moodle by Thursday (16:50-17:00)
Start this alone, in Section 5 of WORKSHEET.md. You now have four required kinds of evidence about unknown_sample: the quick BLAST hit, the deep BLAST table, the alignment and distance table, and the protein-level check. Block D’s 114-tip tree is a fifth, bonus piece of evidence: unknown_sample’s unusually long branch, apart from all 113 real SARS-CoV-2 genomes, is a strong, independent confirmation, by a completely different method, of the same conclusion. Citing it strengthens an answer but is not required. Write:

a conclusion answering today’s biological question for unknown_sample, citing evidence from at least two of the four required sources by name (block D’s tree can count as a bonus third or more);
one sentence naming a limitation, uncertainty, or assumption in today’s analysis (the block B/C disagreement over MERS-CoV versus HCoV-OC43_seasonal is one honest candidate, but not the only one).

Get a complete draft down before you leave; a clear, unrushed final version, in your own words, is due on Moodle by Thursday.


3.3.9 Wrap-up
Save your script, confirm results/ contains both BLAST tables, blastp_result.tsv, sars_variants_tree_mine.nwk, and your exported tree image. Submit WORKSHEET.md plus the tree image through Moodle by Thursday: any file format works for the image (PNG, JPEG, PDF, SVG, …), and WORKSHEET.md can be submitted as-is (plain text/Markdown) or converted to PDF or Word first if you prefer — Moodle accepts any of these, there is no required file type beyond “readable.”

3.5 Optional challenge
For your own interest, not graded.
A. Root on a background tip instead. In plot_tree.R, set root_on to one of the unlabelled background accessions instead of unknown_sample (grep ">" sars_variants.fasta for options). Does this change the named variants’ grouping at all? Why might rooting on unknown_sample (as the script does by default, confirmed as a real outgroup by its long branch and by blocks B-D2) give a more defensible picture than rooting on an arbitrary background sequence, even though both are valid trees mathematically?
B. A distance correction model. Today’s small tree (blocks B-D2) used raw percent difference as its distance. Try a correction model that accounts for multiple substitutions at the same site:
library(ape)
aln <- read.dna("aligned_spike.fasta", format = "fasta")
d_raw <- dist.dna(aln, model = "raw", pairwise.deletion = TRUE)
d_jc <- dist.dna(aln, model = "JC69", pairwise.deletion = TRUE)
round(as.matrix(d_raw)["unknown_sample", ] * 100, 1)
round(as.matrix(d_jc)["unknown_sample", ] * 100, 1)
The closest reference barely moves under the correction; the two most distant ones move a lot more. Given the “saturation” idea from the theory block, why would correction matter more for distant pairs than for close ones? (FastTree’s own log, printed to the screen each time you ran it today, names the distance it starts from: look for the word “Jukes-Cantor” near the top.)

text:
Bonus: a rigorous tree, for real (IQ-TREE)






TipOptional, for students who are ahead



This is not part of the course. No marks depend on it, and no later session assumes you have done it. It exists because the theory block named two things FastTree approximates for speed, a proper substitution model and real bootstrap support, and leaves them “out of scope.” This bonus is that scope, on the exact same alignment you already have.


FastTree assumed a simple substitution model (Jukes-Cantor: every base equally likely to mutate into every other) and estimates support with a fast approximation (SH-like, roughly “how often does this split survive small random tweaks”). IQ-TREE does both properly, at real computational cost: ModelFinder tests dozens of substitution models (different rules for how often each base swaps for each other one, whether some sites mutate faster than others) and picks the one that fits your data best by a statistical criterion, then ultrafast bootstrap rebuilds the tree 1,000 times, each time from a random resample of the alignment’s columns, and reports what fraction of those 1,000 trees agree with each split in the final one. That is what a bootstrap support value (typically written as a percentage, out of 100) actually counts.

3.6.1 Try it (1-2 minutes to run)
module load IQ-TREE
iqtree3 -s aligned_spike.fasta -m MFP -B 1000 -T AUTO --prefix ../results/iqtree_bonus
-m MFP runs ModelFinder before building anything. -B 1000 requests 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates. -T AUTO lets IQ-TREE pick how many threads to use.






NoteCheckpoint



This takes noticeably longer than FastTree, roughly a minute or two on LEGcompute, not under a second: proper model selection and 1,000 real resamples cost real time. When it finishes, ../results/iqtree_bonus.iqtree is a full text report; the one line to find is “Best-fit model according to BIC”. ../results/iqtree_bonus.treefile is the tree itself, in Newick format exactly like FastTree’s output, except each internal split is now labelled with a number out of 100 rather than FastTree’s 0-1 scale.


Open plot_tree.R, duplicate the line that reads the tree, and point the copy at "../results/iqtree_bonus.treefile" instead, to plot this one the same way. Two questions worth answering for yourself, not submitted anywhere:

Is the topology (which sequences group together) the same as your FastTree tree?
Are the bootstrap values close to FastTree’s support values, or different? Given that one is a fast approximation and the other resamples the data 1,000 times, what would you expect, and why might a real difference (if you see one) matter more on a harder dataset than on this one?



3.6.2 Go further
Open ../results/iqtree_bonus.iqtree in a text editor and find the “SUBSTITUTION PROCESS” section near the end, where “Rate parameter R” and “State frequencies” sit a few lines below the model name. These are the actual numbers ModelFinder fit to your data: for example, how much more often a transition (A<->G or C<->T) happens than a transversion, for these five coronavirus spike genes specifically, rather than assumed equal as FastTree’s default model assumes.







NoteSources and reuse





The four named reference sequences are real NCBI RefSeq records, fetched directly for this course, both as nucleotide CDS and as protein: SARS-CoV-2 (NC_045512.2, protein YP_009724390.1), SARS-CoV-1 (NC_004718.3, protein YP_009825051.1), MERS-CoV (NC_019843.3, protein YP_009047204.1), and HCoV-OC43 (NC_006213.1, protein YP_009555241.1). unknown_sample is a fifth real NCBI record, also a spike gene; its accession is kept out of this public page on purpose, since it is this session’s graded unknown. The alignment was built with MAFFT (--auto), precomputed so that the practical starts from a correct result. The SARS-CoV-2 protein accession (P0DTC2 in UniProt, YP_009724390.1 in NCBI) is the same record included in Session 1’s mystery.fasta. The bonus section’s iqtree_bonus run uses IQ-TREE’s ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap on this same alignment. Block D’s 114-tip tree is fetched live from NCBI by students themselves (100 arbitrary SARS-CoV-2 genomes plus 13 named variants, listed in block D, plus unknown_sample itself, added back in to check blocks B-D2’s conclusion by an independent method); sars_variants_aligned.fasta and sars_variants_tree.nwk are that same live pipeline (EntrezDirect, MAFFT --auto, FastTree -nt), run once ahead of time and kept only as a fallback. None of this is authored by this course; see NCBI, UniProt, and the ape, MAFFT, FastTree, EntrezDirect, and IQ-TREE documentation for the original data and tools.
